# Taking Advantage of a Rare Opportunity in Hedged Equity


October 22, 2026


[Calamos Hedged Equity Fund (CIHEX)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/mutual/hedged-equity-cihex/) and[Calamos Active Hedged Equity ETF (CHDG)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/etf/calamos-active-hedged-equity-chdg/)


[Dave O’Donohue](https://www.calamos.com/about/portfolio-management/david-odonohue/) , Co-Head of Alternative Strategies, Senior Co-Portfolio Manager


## Summary Points


We believe:


- A flexible approach gives[Calamos Hedged Equity Fund (CIHEX)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/mutual/hedged-equity-cihex/) and[Calamos Active Hedged Equity ETF (CHDG)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/etf/calamos-active-hedged-equity-chdg/) a real edge over systematic hedged equity strategies.
- We took advantage of an extraordinary opportunity this month—one that we haven’t seen in decades.
- CIHEX’s and CHDG’s hedges set up well for equity investors concerned about market risk.


We recently adjusted the hedge in CIHEX and CHDG. We believe our ability to jump on this unique opportunity is a powerful example of what our active hedged equity approach can do. Below, we walk through what we did, why we did it, and what we would expect along the way.


## Q. What changed?


A. We rolled our existing hedge into a slightly different structure, using December 2028 expirations and strikes closer to the current spot price. Previously, we were selling about 35% in calls and buying about 65% in at-the-money puts. Now we are selling only approximately 28% in calls and were able to buy approximately 72% notional in puts. We also resized and reset each fund’s short put leg, rolling it out to December 2028 on about 32% of notional with a strike about 30% out of the money. This still leaves us with net puts of around 40%.


## Q. Is it a material difference?


A. It is still the same core trade as our 65/35, so we do not see it as a material shift; however, it is change that we are excited about. The slightly different structure and the longer-dated expirations bring different benefits and risks, which we’ll explain below.


## Q. Why now?


A. The 2-year Treasury yield rose from 3.47% to almost 5% this year, while longer-dated volatility stayed fairly low. Higher rates make the calls we sell more valuable and the puts we buy cheaper, and low volatility keeps the absolute cost of the puts lower. Together, those two things brought the price of this hedge to a level we have seen rarely, if ever, in the last 20 years (see the chart below). We see this as a unique opportunity to lock in a hedge with the kind of asymmetry that suits investors looking for equity upside with less potential downside.

## Q. What are the potential benefits?


A. We believe moving out to 2028 lets us improve on the 65/35 profile we had before. We think the new structure could capture 70% or more of the market's upside with 30% or less of its downside over the life of the hedge, through December 2028. Additionally, since we have put a profile we like in place for a longer period, it gives us maximum flexibility going forward. We can let an unusually attractive hedge run its course, but we can always adjust it further if an even better opportunity emerges.


One caveat: this 70/30 ***is a target* for the full life of the structure** . Along the way, the hedge is marked to market, so the options reflect the time remaining, volatility, and interest rates, in addition to the level of the S&P 500. If the options are held to expiration, their payoff at expiration supports the 70/30 target described above. In the short run, we would expect somewhat higher downside capture and lower upside capture than the target. Moving the hedge out to two years lengthens that early window, so results over shorter periods may look different from what we expect over the full life of the structure. This is typical of a longer-dated hedge, and in our view, strengthens the case for thinking of CIHEX and CHDG as strategies to use as part of a long-term allocation.


## Q. Why short puts, too?


A. We continue to believe the short put leg makes sense, in some capacity, for two reasons. First, it gives us another way to benefit from our active approach. We do not have to sell the same amount as our long puts, and we do not have to sell them on the same day we buy the long puts, so we can use market moves and changes in volatility to adjust opportunistically. By selling puts during periods of stress or down markets and buying them back during periods of complacent or rising markets, we can generate realized profits and/or improve the funds’ return profiles over time. Second, because the short put is struck about 30% below the market, it makes the funds more long-leaning after a large selloff. We do not believe in systematically capping our put position, which leaves a large unhedged part of the downside distribution, but we do think hedged equity investors want to slowly increase participation after selloffs, and this structure gives us a way to do that.


## Q. What does this new hedge mean for CIHEX and CHDG?


A. We believe this is a great example of why active hedged equity is the right route and that this is a particularly attractive time for these strategies. The market gives different things at different times, and right now it is offering an unusually good opportunity for asymmetry. For investors who are worried about the equity risk or where we are in the market cycle, we believe CIHEX and CHDG can make it easier to stay in equities but pull back a bit on downside risk exposure.
